summary: Specifies how Deterministic Networking (DetNet) service works for IP traffic on IP hosts and routers. No new DetNet header is defined for IP flows. Instead, existing IP and higher-layer header information is used to identify flows and deliver the service.

plainLanguage.summary: Deterministic Networking is about giving some traffic a guaranteed, very small chance of loss and a guaranteed upper bound on delay. This document asks how to do that with ordinary IP packets, without adding a new header. The answer is that the network recognises the special traffic from the addresses, ports and priority bits already in the packet, and then treats it the way the operator asked.

questions: how does detnet work over ip
how does detnet identify ip flows
does detnet ip provide packet replication
subtitle: How IP routers and hosts give deterministic service to flows by recognizing them from ordinary IP and port fields.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking promises extremely low packet loss and assured maximum latency, and the network needs a way to tell which IP packets belong to such a flow.
tldr.mechanism: No DetNet-specific header is added. Nodes match existing IP and transport header fields, mainly the 6-tuple, against provisioned flow information and give matching packets the configured treatment.
tldr.outcome: DetNet service works with unmodified IP packets, but it gives only the forwarding sub-layer, so service protection is per sub-network and not end to end.

today: RFC 8939 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the DetNet IP data plane specification, sitting alongside the common data plane model in RFC 8938 and the DetNet architecture in RFC 8655.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking is a service that can be offered by a network to DetNet flows. DetNet provides these flows with extremely low packet loss rates and assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. This document specifies the DetNet data plane operation for IP hosts and routers that provide DetNet service to IP-encapsulated data. No DetNet-specific encapsulation is defined to support IP flows; instead, the existing IP-layer and higher-layer protocol header information is used to support flow identification and DetNet service delivery.

The DetNet architecture models the DetNet-related data plane functions as two sub-layers: a service sub-layer and a forwarding sub-layer. The service sub-layer is used to provide DetNet service protection, for example by the Packet Replication Function and Packet Elimination Function, and reordering. The forwarding sub-layer is used to provide congestion protection: low loss, assured latency, and limited out-of-order delivery. The service sub-layer generally requires additional header fields to provide its service. Since no DetNet-specific fields are added to support DetNet IP flows, only the forwarding sub-layer functions are supported using the DetNet IP defined by this document. Service protection can be provided on a per-sub-network basis using technologies such as MPLS and Ethernet, as specified by the IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking task group.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet has two jobs. The forwarding job is to keep the path free: low loss, tight delay, little reordering. The service job is to protect the traffic itself, by sending copies down two paths and throwing away the duplicate later. The service job normally needs extra header fields to do its work, and this document adds none, so over plain IP only the forwarding job is available.

sections.title: Overview of the DetNet IP Data Plane
sections.content:
The DetNet IP data plane primarily uses 6-tuple-based flow identification, where the 6-tuple refers to information carried in IP-layer and higher-layer protocol headers. The 6-tuple is the destination address, source address, IP protocol, source port, destination port and DSCP. A 6-tuple is composed of a 5-tuple plus the addition of a DSCP component. For some protocols, 5-tuples and 6-tuples cannot be used, because the port information is not available, for example with ICMP, IPsec and Encapsulating Security Payload; this is also the case for flow aggregates. In such cases, using fewer fields is appropriate, such as a 3-tuple of two IP addresses and the IP protocol, or even a 2-tuple of all IP traffic between two IP addresses. The data plane also allows for optional matching on the IPv6 Flow Label field.

Non-DetNet and DetNet IP packets have the same protocol header format on the wire, and generally the fields used in flow identification are forwarded unmodified, though standard modification of the DSCP field is not precluded. DetNet flow aggregation may be enabled via the use of wildcards, masks, lists, prefixes and ranges, and IP tunnels may also be used to support flow aggregation.

The first figure illustrates a DetNet-enabled IP network in which the end systems originate IP-encapsulated traffic that is identified within the DetNet domain as DetNet flows based on IP header information. Relay nodes understand the forwarding requirements of the DetNet flow and ensure that node, interface and sub-network resources are allocated to ensure the service requirements. The dotted line around the Service component of the relay nodes indicates that the transit routers are DetNet service aware but do not perform any DetNet service sub-layer function.

The second figure illustrates a variant where the end systems are not DetNet aware. Edge nodes sit at the boundary of the DetNet domain and provide DetNet service proxies for the end applications by initiating and terminating DetNet service for the application's IP flows. Because non-DetNet and DetNet IP packets have the same header format on the wire, from a data plane perspective the only difference is that there is flow-associated DetNet information on each DetNet node that defines the flow-related characteristics and required forwarding behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is recognised by its two addresses, the protocol, the two ports and the priority marking. Some protocols have no ports, so those are recognised with fewer fields. Nothing is added to the packet: a DetNet packet looks exactly like any other, and all the extra information sits in each node's configuration. The second figure covers the case where the applications themselves know nothing about DetNet, and an edge node stands in for them.

sections.title: End-System Considerations
sections.content:
Data flows requiring DetNet service are generated and terminated on end systems. The protocols used by an IP end system are specific to an application, and end systems peer with other end systems. DetNet's use of 6-tuple IP flow identification means that DetNet must be aware of not only the format of the IP header but also of the next protocol value carried within an IP packet.

For DetNet-unaware IP end systems, service-level proxy functions are needed inside the DetNet domain. When IP end systems are DetNet aware, no application-level or service-level proxy functions are needed inside the domain. End systems need to ensure that DetNet service requirements are met when processing packets associated with a DetNet flow. When sending packets, this means that packets are appropriately shaped on transmission and receive appropriate traffic treatment on the connected sub-network. When receiving packets, this means that there are appropriate local node resources, such as buffers, to receive and process the packets of that DetNet flow.

An important additional consideration for DetNet-aware end systems is avoiding IP fragmentation. Full 6-tuple flow identification is not possible on IP fragments, as fragments do not include the transport headers or their port information. It is therefore important that applications and end systems use an IP packet size that will avoid fragmentation within the network when sending DetNet flows. The maximum size can be learned via Path MTU Discovery or via the Controller Plane. Path MTU Discovery relies on ICMP, which may not follow the same path as an individual DetNet flow. In order to maximize reuse of existing mechanisms, DetNet-aware applications and end systems SHOULD NOT mix DetNet and non-DetNet traffic within a single 5-tuple.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical warnings for the sending application. First, do not let the packet be fragmented, because a fragment carries no port numbers and so cannot be recognised as belonging to the flow. Second, do not mix ordinary and deterministic traffic in the same connection, because the network cannot then tell which is which.

sections.title: Domain Considerations and Service Protection
sections.content:
DetNet IP domains need to be able to forward any DetNet flow identified by the IP 6-tuple. Doing otherwise would limit the number of 6-tuple flow ID combinations that could be used by the end systems. This means that all nodes along the end-to-end path of DetNet flows need to agree on what fields are used for flow identification. Possible consequences of not having such an agreement include some flows interfering with other flows, and the traffic treatment expected for a service not being provided.

From a connection-type perspective, two scenarios are identified. In the DN attached case, the end system is directly connected to an edge node or the end system is behind a sub-network. In the DN integrated case, the end system is part of the DetNet domain. A DetNet domain allows communication between any end systems using the same encapsulation format, independent of their connection type and DetNet capability. DN-attached end systems have no knowledge about the DetNet domain and its encapsulation format.

The DetNet-enabled IP routers within a domain are DetNet relays, and they identify DetNet flows based on the IP 6-tuple and ensure that the traffic treatment required by the DetNet service is provided on both the node and any attached sub-network. This solution provides DetNet functions end to end, but it does so on a per-link and per-sub-network basis. Congestion protection, latency control and resource allocation are supported using the underlying link and sub-network-specific mechanisms. However, service protection is not provided end to end at the DetNet layer. Instead, service protection can be provided on a per-link and per-sub-network basis.

Service protection must be implemented within each link and sub-network independently, using the domain-specific mechanisms, due to the lack of unified end-to-end sequencing information that could be used by the intermediate nodes. If end-to-end service protection is desired, it can be implemented by the DetNet end systems using layer 4 transport protocols or application protocols, but those protocols are out of the scope of this document. Not mixing DetNet and non-DetNet traffic within a single 5-tuple enables simpler 5-tuple filters to be used at the edges of a DetNet network to prevent non-congestion-responsive DetNet traffic from escaping the DetNet domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node on the path has to agree on how flows are recognised, or the traffic will not get the treatment it was promised. The important limit is that copying a packet down two paths and deleting the duplicate needs shared sequence information that plain IP does not carry. So duplication can be done inside each link or sub-network, but not across the whole path. An application that needs end-to-end protection has to arrange it itself.

sections.title: Flow Aggregation and Reserved Traffic
sections.content:
The ability to aggregate individual flows and their associated resource control into a larger aggregate is an important technique for improving scaling by reducing the state per hop. DetNet IP data plane aggregation can take place within a single node, when that node maintains state about both the aggregated and individual flows, and between nodes, when one node maintains state about only flow aggregates while the other maintains state on all or a portion of the component flows. The management or control function that provisions the aggregate flows must ensure that adequate resources are allocated and configured to provide the combined service requirements of the individual flows. As DetNet is concerned about latency and jitter, more than just bandwidth needs to be considered.

DetNet IP flows can be aggregated using any of the 6-tuple fields and optionally also by the flow label. The use of prefixes, wildcards, lists and value ranges allows a DetNet node to identify aggregate DetNet flows. From a resource allocation perspective, DetNet nodes ought to provide service to an aggregate rather than on a component flow basis. It is the responsibility of the DetNet Controller Plane to properly provision the use of these aggregation mechanisms, including ensuring that aggregated flows have compatible QoS and CoS characteristics, and that per-component-flow service requirements are satisfied by the aggregate.

Quality of Service for DetNet service flows carried in IP must be provided locally by the DetNet-aware hosts and routers supporting DetNet flows, leveraging the underlying network layer such as 802.1 TSN. Packets that are identified as part of a DetNet IP flow but that have not been the subject of a completed reservation can disrupt the QoS offered to properly reserved DetNet flows by using resources allocated to the reserved flows. The network nodes of a DetNet network MUST therefore ensure that no DetNet-allocated resource, such as a queue or shaper, is used by such flows. Several methods may be used, including treating packets associated with an incomplete reservation as non-DetNet traffic, discarding them, or re-marking them by changing the value of the DSCP field to a value that results in the packet no longer matching any other reserved DetNet IP flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserving resources for many flows at once saves the routers work, and the network can group flows using prefixes, wildcards, lists and ranges. The risk is a flow that looks like a reserved one but was never actually reserved; if it is allowed to use the reserved queue, the reserved traffic suffers. The document lists three ways to stop that, including re-marking the packet so it no longer matches.

sections.title: Flow Identification Procedures
sections.content:
All DetNet implementations that support this document MUST identify individual DetNet flows based on the set of information identified in this section. The configuration and control information used to identify an individual DetNet flow MUST be ordered by an implementation, and implementations MUST support a fixed order when identifying flows and MUST identify a DetNet flow by the first set of matching flow information. Implementations MUST support DetNet flow identification whether they are acting as a DetNet end system, a relay node or an edge node.

Implementations MUST support flow identification based on the IPv4 Source Address and the IPv6 Source Address, and SHOULD support longest prefix matching for these fields; a prefix length of zero effectively means that the field is ignored. The same applies to the destination address fields, and any IP address value is allowed, including an IP multicast destination address.

Implementations MUST support flow identification based on the IPv4 Protocol field and the IPv6 Next Header field, including the next protocol values defined for the other protocols and any other value, including zero, and SHOULD allow for these fields to be ignored for a specific DetNet flow. They MUST support flow identification based on the DSCP field in the IPv4 Type of Service field and in the IPv6 Traffic Class field, and MUST support list-based matching of DSCP values.

Implementations SHOULD support identification of DetNet flows based on the IPv6 Flow Label field, and implementations that support matching on it MUST allow for it to be ignored for a specific DetNet flow. When it is used, implementations MAY exclude the IPv6 Next Header field and next header information from flow identification.

Implementations MUST support flow identification based on the Source and Destination Port fields of TCP and UDP packets, with exact-value matching required and range-based port matching recommended, and the field must be allowed to be ignored for a specific flow. Flow identification for ICMP is achieved based on the protocol number in the IP header, and ICMP type is not included in the flow definition. IPsec Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload share a common format for the Security Parameters Index field, and implementations MUST support flow identification based on a particular value carried in that field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node holds an ordered list of flow definitions and matches a packet against them in order, taking the first that fits. The definitions can be as loose as a whole address range or as tight as a single port. Every field can also be ignored, which is how one flow can be carved out of a larger aggregate.

sections.title: Forwarding and Traffic Treatment
sections.content:
General requirements for IP nodes are defined elsewhere and are not modified by this document. The typical next-hop selection process is impacted by DetNet: implementations of this document SHALL use management and control information to select the one or more outgoing interfaces and next hops to be used for a packet associated with a DetNet flow. The use of multiple paths or links, for example equal-cost multipath, to support a single DetNet flow is NOT RECOMMENDED. Equal-cost multipath MAY be used for non-DetNet flows within a DetNet domain.

Implementations must ensure that a DetNet flow receives the traffic treatment that is provisioned for it via configuration or the Controller Plane. Typical mechanisms used to provide different treatment to different flows include the allocation of system resources, such as queues and buffers, and provisioning of related parameters, such as shaping and policing. Support can also be provided via an underlying network technology such as MPLS or IEEE 802.1 TSN.

The information needed to identify individual and aggregated DetNet flows is summarised in the document and MUST be provisioned per DetNet flow via configuration, for example via the Controller Plane or the management plane. An implementation MUST support ordering of that information, which can for example be used to provide a DetNet service for a specific UDP flow with unique source and destination port values, while providing a different service for the aggregate of all other flows with that same UDP destination port value. It is the responsibility of the DetNet Controller Plane to properly provision both the flow identification information and the flow-specific resources needed to provide the traffic treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flow is given a path, a queue and a rate, and the node follows the instructions rather than choosing the usual route. One rule stands out: a deterministic flow should not be spread over several equal-cost paths, because that risks reordering, which is exactly what the flow is paying to avoid. Equal-cost multipath is still fine for ordinary traffic inside the same network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Detailed security considerations for DetNet are cataloged separately, and this section exclusively considers security considerations that are specific to the DetNet IP data plane. Security aspects that are unique to DetNet are those whose aim is to provide the specific QoS aspects of DetNet, which are primarily to deliver data flows with extremely low packet loss rates and bounded end-to-end delivery latency. Achieving such loss rates and bounded latency may not be possible in the face of a highly capable adversary, such as the one envisioned by the Internet Threat Model that can arbitrarily drop or delay any or all traffic. In order to present meaningful security considerations, the document considers a somewhat weaker attacker who does not control the physical links of the DetNet domain but may have the ability to control a network node within the boundary of the domain.

The primary consideration for the DetNet data plane is to maintain the integrity of data and the delivery of the associated DetNet service. Since no DetNet-specific fields are available in the DetNet IP data plane, the integrity and confidentiality of application flows can be protected through whatever means are provided by the underlying technology, for example encryption such as that provided by IPsec for IP flows, or by an underlying sub-network using MACsec for IP over Ethernet flows. From a data plane perspective, this document does not add or modify any header information.

At the management and control level, DetNet flows are identified on a per-flow basis, which may provide Controller Plane attackers with additional information about the data flows, when compared to Controller Planes that do not include per-flow identification. To provide uninterrupted availability of the DetNet service, provisions can be made against denial-of-service attacks and delay attacks. To protect against denial-of-service attacks, excess traffic due to malicious or malfunctioning devices can be prevented or mitigated, for example through the use of existing mechanisms such as policing and shaping applied at the input of a DetNet domain or within an edge 802.1 TSN domain. To prevent DetNet packets from being delayed by an entity external to a DetNet domain, the technology definitions can allow for the mitigation of man-in-the-middle attacks, for example through the use of authentication and authorization of devices within the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Very low loss and a tight delay bound are hard promises to keep if somebody controls the network, so the document narrows the attacker to one who can take over a node but not the physical links. The packet format carries nothing extra, so confidentiality has to come from the usual places, such as IPsec or MACsec. And because the controller plane knows about each flow separately, it also knows more about the traffic than a controller plane that does not.

viz.caption: The two DetNet sub-layers, and what plain IP can offer

layers.label: Service sub-layer
layers.detail: Packet replication, elimination and ordering. Needs extra header fields, so it is not available over plain IP.

layers.label: Forwarding sub-layer
layers.detail: Congestion protection: low loss, assured latency, limited reordering.

layers.label: IP
layers.detail: Ordinary IP packets, unmodified on the wire.

layers.label: Sub-network
layers.detail: Ethernet, MPLS or 802.1 TSN, which may provide service protection locally.

viz.caption: The header fields used to recognise a DetNet IP flow

items.title: Source address
items.text: Longest prefix matching is recommended. A prefix length of zero means the field is ignored.

items.title: Destination address
items.text: Longest prefix matching is recommended. Any address value is allowed, including multicast.

items.title: IP protocol or next header
items.text: Required to be supported, and the field must be allowed to be ignored for a given flow.

items.title: Source port
items.text: Exact matching required, range matching recommended, for TCP and UDP.

items.title: Destination port
items.text: Exact matching required, range matching recommended, for TCP and UDP.

items.title: DSCP
items.text: Taken from the IPv4 Type of Service or IPv6 Traffic Class field. List-based matching is required.

items.title: IPv6 flow label
items.text: Optional. When used, it can replace the next header field in the flow definition.
